name: Bhai Kanhaiya
role: Sikh water-bearer remembered for serving all
summary: Bhai Kanhaiya (1648–1718) is remembered for giving water to wounded soldiers on both sides during a siege of Anandpur, and for founding the Sewapanthi order of selfless service.
about: Bhai Kanhaiya was born in 1648 at Sodhara near Wazirabad, in a wealthy Dhamman Khatri family. He is said to have given to the poor from a young age, and he became a follower of Guru Tegh Bahadur, serving as water-carrier and in the kitchen. Sikh tradition says that during a siege of Anandpur in the early 1700s (sources say 1703, 1704 or 1705) he carried water to wounded soldiers, friend and enemy alike. When Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh, he answered that he saw only people (the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism words it as the Guru's face in everyone), and the Guru blessed him. The Guru sent him to Sindh, and his order became known as Sewapanthi. He died in 1718.
kidSummary: Bhai Kanhaiya carried a water bag across a battlefield and gave a drink to anyone who was thirsty, even soldiers on the other side. When asked why, he said he only saw people who needed help. Guru Gobind Singh blessed him.

story.title: A kind boy
story.text: Kanhaiya came from a rich family in Sodhara, but gave to the poor from a young age. Later he joined the Sikhs and served Guru Tegh Bahadur.

story.title: Serving the Gurus
story.text: He carried water, worked in the kitchen and looked after horses. After Guru Tegh Bahadur, he served Guru Gobind Singh.

story.title: The siege
story.text: When enemy forces attacked Anandpur, Bhai Kanhaiya walked among the fallen with a goatskin bag of water and gave drinks to the wounded.

story.title: The complaint
story.text: Some Sikh fighters told the Guru he was also helping the enemy. The Guru asked him why.

story.title: Only people
story.text: Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw no friend or foe, only people who were thirsty. Guru Gobind Singh blessed him and gave him medicine to help the wounded.

story.title: A path of service
story.text: The Guru sent him to Sindh. His followers, the Sewapanthis, made serving others their way of life.

teaches: Help anyone in need, friend or stranger

facts.text: When a new head of a Sewapanthi centre, called a tikana, is chosen, he is given a broom and a bowl. The broom stands for cleanliness and the bowl for serving others.
Sewapanthis kept serving the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar even during the harsh persecution under governor Zakariya Khan, and they did it by keeping its inner lamp lit.

During a siege of Anandpur he carried a goatskin water bag and gave water to everyone who was thirsty. The Sewapanthi page says the wounded he helped included enemy hill troops, Mughal soldiers from the Sirhind region, and Gujjar and Pathan irregulars.

Some Sikh fighters complained to Guru Gobind Singh that he helped the enemy too. Wikipedia says he answered that he saw only people; the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says he saw the Guru's face in everyone.
The Guru is said to have given him a medicine chest, a bed and a handkerchief, and to have blessed him by saying that a Sikh order would follow after him.
The sect prepared special ink used to copy Sikh scriptures by hand, called Roshanai or Addanshahi ink.
He preached sitting on a cot, so people in Sindh called him Khat Waro Bao and Khaatwala Baba, the cot-sitting elder. The Khat Wari Darbar in Shikarpur is a temple dedicated to him.

Sikh writers often call him a forerunner of the Red Cross. Henry Dunant's ideas, which grew out of the battle of Solferino in 1859, came about 155 years after the Anandpur siege, though Sikhchic describes the gap as almost two centuries.

Sikhchic reports that the Punjab health department once told civil hospitals to name their emergency wards after him, and a charity called the Bhai Kanhaiya Mission runs dispensaries, day-care centres and blood donation camps.

In 2011 the SGPC, the Punjab government and the Delhi Sikh gurdwara committee each wrote to the International Committee of the Red Cross, asking it to recognise his service to the wounded in its own literature.
In the Sikh Missionary Society's retelling, he explained his action by pointing to the scripture's teaching that nobody is an enemy or a stranger, and the Guru praised him as a true Sikh.
He first met Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur when he was ten and again at sixteen. He was so taken with the Guru's mission that he never married, thinking a family would take time away from serving.
The Guru is said to have given him a seli topi as a reward. He is remembered as humble and wore plain clothes that he made himself.
Sewapanthis are pacifists who do not harm other living beings, yet they accept in principle that the Khalsa may have to fight to protect dharma, and many chose not to take the Khalsa initiation.
Sewapanthis do not live by begging or alms. They make useful goods and sell them, a habit the page traces to a teacher named Aya Ram and his disciple Dharam Das.
Because they lived among Sindhi communities, Sewapanthis often read Sufi and Islamic literature as well as Sikh writings.
Sewapanthi saints are said to have supervised the building of the langar hall of the Golden Temple, the huge free kitchen that feeds visitors.

The Addanshahi name comes from his disciple Addan Shah, who began as an Udasi and a student of Baba Gurdas Dakhani. The page also calls Kanhaiya himself an Udasi and says the two orders have stayed close.
Paras Ram, a Sewapanthi who had a disability and was called a pingla, founded a Sewapanthi service centre in the Jangi Shiva Bazaar of Amritsar.
Many Sewapanthis were sehajdhari Sikhs without a Khalsa look, so they could go on writing Sikh books while Khalsa Sikhs were hunted. They call their collected life stories parchai, not sakhis.
The Sewapanthi page says the order's name means a fellowship or path of service, and that its members aim to overcome selfishness through service done with respect and love.

quiz.q: What did Bhai Kanhaiya carry on the battlefield?
quiz.why: He carried a goatskin water bag.

quiz.q: Who did he give water to?
quiz.why: He helped friend and enemy alike.

quiz.q: What does the title Khatwala Baba mean?
quiz.why: People called him Khatwala Baba because he sat on a cot to preach.
